english.html: semblance, accompanied by a thousand frauds and lies, some men born in poor, low and humble station have known how to practise so well that they persuaded a whole people that they were sprung of a great, noble and illustrious race: as a Smerdis, an Archelaus, an Equitius, a Herophilus, and several others, whose history will be told below in a more convenient place. Nevertheless, if the circumstances are measured by a true ell and weighed in a just balance, this deed will appear incomparably more monstrous and astonishing than all the others: in none of which will it be found that such a likeness, though it was painted over and clothed in a thousand necessary lies, was so powerful as to impose upon all the kinsfolk, and even upon four sisters, and upon the uncle who had brought up the nephew from his childhood, as in this present case — nay (what must draw everyone into still greater wonder), upon the wife herself, who received another man for her husband, and with him conversed familiarly, as husband and wife do, for the space of three years and more, without ever perceiving, nor even suspecting, the fraud. Although in other substitutions women have often shown themselves sharper, quicker and more perspicacious in discovering and detecting them than men: as the history of the wife of Quintus Sertorius at Rome, and of Jeanne, daughter of Count Baldwin in Flanders, will well bear witness, as we shall relate more fully hereafter a. And touching the great likenesses that there have been between certain men, there have been several in the past, of which some were maintained without fraud, and others produced great and notable impostures. As to the first: once at Rome, Vibius and Publicius, persons of very low and base condition, so closely resembled the great Pompey that the Romans called them Pompeys, and sometimes named Pompey Vibius or Publicius b. A like resemblance was between Cornelius Scipio and a swineherd (or, according to others, a victimarius, that is to say, a dealer in beasts for sacrifice) who was called Serapion c. Likewise between Hybreas the Milesian, that great and renowned orator, and a slave whom history does not name — so much so that the ancients firmly believed that they were brothers d. To Mark Antony, in his

notes.gloss: The wife of Sertorius and Jeanne of Flanders are told at once in Annotation VII below; the reference forward is to Coras's later treatment of the same examples.

notes.citation: Pliny, Natural History VII.10 (§53–54; Coras's c. 12 follows the old chapter division); Solinus, Collectanea rerum memorabilium 1 (Inter Cnaeum Pompeium et Cn. Vibium, humili loco natum; Coras's c. 5 not reconciled with the modern chapter division)
notes.original: Pline au li ure vij. c. xij. Solin en ſon Polihiſto. c. v.
notes.gloss: Vibius, a plebeian, and Publicius, a freedman, so like Pompey that the crowd gave them his name.

notes.citation: Valerius Maximus, Memorable Doings and Sayings IX.14 (De similitudine formae; Coras's c. 15, the old numbering); Pliny and Solinus as above
notes.original: Valere le Grand au li, ix. c. xv. Pline & Sol. ou deſ ſus.
notes.gloss: Valerius says Scipio got the by-name Serapion from a victimarius's slave; Pliny makes Serapion the slave of a pig-dealer. Coras gives both.
Valerius has Hybreas of Mylasa (Mylasensis); Coras's "Milesian" is his own or his edition's slip.
